01-the-liquidity-lie.easy_to_get: S — the claim lands in the second paragraph: obvious levels are hunting grounds, and if you cannot see the sweep you are the liquidity. Title, hook and Part 1 all point the same way.

02-volume-doesnt-lie.delivers: S — all four objectives land: delta, the two patterns, the three profile components, Plutus Flow.

02-volume-doesnt-lie.easy_to_get: S — opens on a concrete puzzle (two identical volume bars, opposite outcomes) and answers it immediately: volume is quantity, delta is quality. A 'Quick Definition: what is delta' block sits BEFORE the case study, which is the right order and rare.
02-volume-doesnt-lie.evidence: A — was D. The '🔄 Recovery' box asserting a 74% win rate and +$65,000 is gone; the New Rules list it wrapped, which is the actual payload, stayed. 'Print money' (which five of eleven locales had already quietly softened) and 'every single one of 47 trades' are both out.
strengths: Definition-before-demonstration, done properly
The absorption/exhaustion table is the clearest thing in the beginner tier
Each profile component gets definition, why it matters, how to trade it
02-volume-doesnt-lie.worth_the_time: A — was B. The delta thresholds were absolute (+3,000 / -5,000) with no instrument named, so they were unusable at best and misleading at worst. They now read against the instrument's own typical bar, which is the only way delta means anything.

03-price-action-is-dead.delivers: S — all five objectives are met, including the Volume Oracle regime tie-in that lessons often promise and skip.
03-price-action-is-dead.easy_to_follow: S — was B. 'Cumulative delta' is the case study's entire diagnosis and was not defined until Part 2; it is now defined immediately before the diagnosis relies on it.
03-price-action-is-dead.easy_to_get: A — 'the candle shows WHERE price traded, order flow shows HOW it got there' is a clean thesis, stated in the first three sentences and never lost.
03-price-action-is-dead.evidence: A — was C. The footprint worked example now reconciles: bottom band +4,600, top band -7,970, net -3,370, and the arithmetic checks. It previously claimed the bottom band was +2,210, which was one row's delta from near the TOP with its sign flipped — an error the lesson's own ideal reader would have caught. The tape keeps its second-resolution prints, because a beginner learning to read prints needs to see prints, and gains the word 'illustrative'.
strengths: Thesis is stated in three sentences and holds for the whole lesson
Iceberg mechanics explained from the institution's problem, not as a definition
The three-layer framework gives the reader a repeatable check
weaknesses: The brief HVN/LVN restatement overlaps lesson 2 — kept deliberately: it is short, framed for order flow rather than volume profile, and the corpus-wide check found no shared passage between the two lessons
03-price-action-is-dead.worth_the_time: A — tape reading, footprint, imbalances, iceberg detection and a three-layer confirmation framework. Arguably too deep for the beginner tier: this is the third lesson and it is teaching iceberg detection.

04-repaint-problem.easy_to_follow: S — definition, cost, case, what deterministic means, then the audit framework. Nothing is used before it is explained.
04-repaint-problem.easy_to_get: S — the best opening in the tier. A 9:38 AM scenario, then the definition in one sentence: a signal that moves or vanishes after its bar has closed. Then why that costs you the whole edge.

The red-flag rule is corrected too: a low win rate was never the tell, a curve with no pain in it is.

05-rsi-extremes.delivers: S — all four objectives are met.
05-rsi-extremes.easy_to_follow: A — Part 3 opens with an explicit roadmap ('There are three, and the rest of this lesson is each of them in turn'), which is the best signposting in the tier. Cosmetic: the Part 3 heading runs into the next one with no space.
05-rsi-extremes.easy_to_get: S — gives the correct, deflationary definition of RSI ('recent up-moves have been much larger than recent down-moves, nothing more') and then the thesis: the same reading means three different things in three regimes.
05-rsi-extremes.evidence: A — was C, and the contradiction is resolved. Part 2 warns that any precise figure about algorithm behaviour, 'including one you read here', is a guess dressed up as data; two screens earlier the lesson quoted a win rate to one decimal off 55 trades. That now reads '20 of them winners' — same fact, checkable, no false precision. The $31,800 counterfactual is gone; the measured finding beside it (average rally after her exits) carries the point.
strengths: The RSI definition is correct and deflationary, which is rare
Explicit roadmap sentence before the three scenarios
Part 2's honesty note about unknowable institutional parameters
05-rsi-extremes.worth_the_time: S — goes well past overbought/oversold: regime-dependence, four divergence types, multi-timeframe alignment, and volume/delta confluence.

06-moving-averages.delivers: A — was C, and this was the real defect. One objective claimed crossovers are lagging with '60-80% of move already done' while the body says 20-30% in eleven places, including the arithmetic that derives it and the quiz answer that tests it. Another promised the reader would apply the Pilot Line, which the lesson never explained. A third said 'trade pullbacks TO moving averages' under a title reading Stop Buying the Touch. All three now match the lesson underneath them.
06-moving-averages.easy_to_follow: A — was B. Builds well: myth, then what MAs actually show, then why algos react anyway, then the Golden Cross arithmetic, then the event framework. The one break was 'Pilot Line', a proper noun doing load-bearing work in three of the five event definitions with nothing behind it anywhere on the page; it is now defined before Part 4 leans on it, and the definition earns its place by saying how this line differs from the 50 EMA the lesson has just spent five sections demolishing.
06-moving-averages.easy_to_get: S — the hook is a timestamped 40 seconds (10:18 touch, 10:22 through it, stop gone) and then the claim in plain words: a 50-period EMA is the average of the last fifty closes, no order sits at that number. Title, hook and Part 1 all argue the same thing.
06-moving-averages.evidence: A — was B. The composite's win rate went to counts (16 of 45). The bare '60-70%' algo share now says it is an industry estimate that moves with venue and instrument — which this lesson, three sections from its own model caveat, had no excuse not to do. And 'acting on TD alone = getting faked out 50% of the time' is replaced by what TD actually claims: selling looks exhausted, which is not the same as the reversal having started.
strengths: The Golden Cross lag is derived from the arithmetic, not asserted
Its working-figures caveat is the model the rest of the corpus should follow
The retail-belief vs reality split is concrete and hard to misread
Explains why MAs sometimes 'work' (clustered algo behaviour) without conceding they are support
weaknesses: Four product names (Janus Atlas, Plutus Flow, Volume Oracle, Pentarch) arrive in the Step 3 checklist with one-line glosses — acceptable at lesson 6 because each is cross-linked, but it is the densest product moment in the beginner tier
06-moving-averages.worth_the_time: S — the Golden Cross section is the best thing in the beginner tier. It does not assert the lag, it derives it: a 50-bar average has to cross a 200-bar average, so price must have risen for weeks first. And its stat box carries the caveat the rest of the corpus should copy — 'these are working figures, not a published study … check the lag yourself on the instrument you actually trade.'
